summary: This unit teaches you to manage your time at work and in training: set clear goals, sort tasks by urgency and importance, plan your day and week, use lists, calendars, timers and the appointment book, keep to service times, handle delays, interruptions and requests from others, and review how you spent your time so that you can improve. The examples are from salons, but the methods work in any workplace.

blocks.p: **Time** is the one thing a stylist cannot buy more of. Every client, every service and every task takes a certain amount of it. If you manage it well, clients are served on time, services are done properly and safely, and you finish the day tired but not exhausted. If you manage it badly, clients wait, work is rushed, safety steps are skipped and stress builds.

This unit is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees, but it applies to every job and to your studies as well. It is mostly about **habits and judgement**: what to do first, how to plan, how to say no, and how to keep a record so you can improve.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and practical tasks at the Centre. In the practicals your group plans a busy Saturday on a paper appointment book, and you time a station set-up, find the time wasters and make a personal weekly plan with a SMART goal. A trainee who skips a hygiene or safety step to be faster is not yet competent for that step.

ul: Clients regularly wait a long time past their booking.
Stations are not ready when the client arrives.

blocks.note: Being **punctual** (arriving on time and ready to work) is the first habit of a professional. In Jamaica traffic, late buses and route taxis, and bad weather can delay you. Plan to leave early enough, and tell your supervisor at once if you will be late.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A **goal** is something you want to achieve. A goal without a plan is only a wish. Good goals keep you focused on what matters.

head: Kind of goal
Meaning
Example
rows: Short-term
Done within days or a few weeks
Finish today's practice cuts by 3 p.m.; learn the steps of a roller set this week
Medium-term
Done within a few months
Pass the practical assessment this term
Long-term
Done within a year or more
Complete the qualification; open my own salon in five years

head: Letter
Question to ask
Example
rows: Specific
What exactly do I want to do?
Do a full silk press on a practice head.
Measurable
How will I know when I have done it?
In 90 minutes or less, to the instructor's standard.
Achievable
Can I do it with my time, skill and resources?
I know the steps and only need to get faster; I can practise three times a week.
Relevant
Does it matter for my work or my qualification?
Clients ask for this service and it is part of my unit.
Time-bound
By when?
By the end of next month.

blocks.p: **Weak goal:** 'I want to get better at braiding.' **SMART goal:** 'I will complete a set of knotless braids on a practice head in under 3 hours, neat enough for my instructor to pass, by the end of March, by practising every Wednesday and Saturday.'

blocks.note: Break a big goal into small steps, each with its own date. Tick the steps off as you finish them. You will see progress and stay motivated.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: You will always have more tasks than time. To **prioritise** is to put them in order according to how urgent and how important they are.

ul: **Urgent** means it must be done soon, or there will be a consequence.
**Important** means it matters a lot for clients, safety, your qualification or the business.

head: How important
Urgent
Not urgent
rows: **Important**
Do first
Rinse a relaxer when its time is up
Deal with a client's reaction
Prepare the station for a client due in 10 minutes
Plan time for it
Study for your NVQ-J assessment
Order stock before it runs out
Practise a new technique
**Not important**
Hand over or do quickly
Answer the phone while you are working on a client (the receptionist can)
Reply to a casual message
Limit or drop
Scrolling on your phone
Long chats unrelated to work
Re-arranging shelves for the third time

ul: Do urgent and important tasks first.
Plan regular time for the important but not urgent tasks, such as study and practice. If you do not, they become urgent emergencies later.
Hand over or do quickly the tasks that are urgent but not important.
Cut down the rest.

blocks.p: Your list for the next hour: (a) restock the shelf; (b) prepare the station for a client due in 10 minutes; (c) plan next week's window display. Order: (b) first, because it is urgent and important; (a) next, as it is quick and keeps work running; (c) is important but can wait, so schedule it for a quieter time.

blocks.note: Client safety always comes first. A chemical service timed on the clock cannot wait. Never leave a client with a relaxer or colour to answer the phone or to chat.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Tool
What it does
Tip
rows: To-do list
A list of tasks to complete. Tick them off.
Write it at the start of the day or the night before; put tasks in order of priority; fit small jobs into gaps.
Diary or planner
Shows your week, with dates, appointments, deadlines and study.
Write everything in one place.
Phone calendar and reminders
Sends reminders for bookings, tasks and deadlines.
Set reminders before deadlines, not only at them.
Appointment book or booking system
Plans which client sees which stylist and when.
Keep it up to date; look at it first thing in the morning.
Timer
Tracks processing times, heat times and breaks.
Start it the moment the timed step starts.
Rota
Shows who works when.
Check it each week.
Gantt chart
A chart with tasks down the side and bars along a timeline of days or weeks. It shows when each task starts and finishes and which overlap.
Use it to plan a larger job such as a window display or a show.

ul: **The night before:** check tomorrow's bookings, get your uniform ready, and plan how you will travel, leaving time for traffic.

**On arrival:** set up your station (clean and disinfected tools, fresh towels, products in stock, hot tools checked). Look at the book again for long or chemical services, clients with allergies, and gaps.
**During the day:** keep to the booking times, use a timer for processing, deal politely with interruptions and use gaps for small jobs.
**If you start running late:** tell the receptionist, so that she can warn the next client.
**End of day:** clean up, restock, review the day and plan tomorrow.

blocks.p: Many rotas and schedules use the **24-hour clock**. After 12:00 noon, subtract 12 to get the p.m. time. 15:30 is 3:30 p.m. 08:00 is 8:00 a.m. 18:00 is 6:00 p.m.

ul: To add time, add the minutes first. 2:50 p.m. + 35 minutes: 50 + 35 = 85 minutes = 1 hour 25 minutes, so 3:25 p.m.
1 hour 45 minutes = 105 minutes. 2 hours 30 minutes = 150 minutes.
Work **backwards** from a deadline to find the start time: if a station set-up takes 20 minutes and the salon opens at 8:30 a.m., start at 8:10 a.m.
Hours worked: from 09:00 to 17:00 is 8 hours; take off a 1-hour lunch break for 7 hours of work.
Several stylists at once: when several stylists work at the same time, divide the total work by the number of stylists, and round up if there is some left over.

blocks.note: Always **estimate** (work out in advance) how long a task will take, then compare with the real time. Your estimates will get better.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: The appointment book (on paper or on a computer) is the salon's time plan. A good book keeps clients, stylists and equipment from clashing.

ul: Client's name and phone number
Service or services, and any special note (for example 'skin test done on 4 November' or 'allergy to latex')
Stylist
Date, start time and finish time

blocks.h: Working out how long to book

ul: Use the salon's **list of service times**. Add up every service the client has asked for.
Include shampoo, rinse, drying and finishing, not only the main service.
Add **processing time** for chemical services, as the maker says. Some of this time the stylist can use to serve another client, but only if she will be back on time for the next step.
Add **clean-up and reset time** after each client (often 5 to 15 minutes).
If the client needs a skin (patch) test first, book it **before** the service day, as the maker's instructions say (often 24 to 48 hours before). Do not do the service until the test is passed.
Plan stylists' **breaks** into the book.

blocks.p: Example: colour application 40 minutes + processing 35 minutes + shampoo and conditioning 15 minutes + cut 40 minutes + blow-dry 30 minutes = 160 minutes (2 hours 40 minutes), plus 10 minutes clean-up = 170 minutes (2 hours 50 minutes).

head: Word
Meaning
rows: Double booking
Booking two clients with one stylist at the same time.
Overbooking
Booking more clients than the stylists have time to serve.
Walk-in
A client who arrives without a booking.
No-show
A client who books but does not come and does not call.
Waiting list
A list of clients who would like an earlier or free slot.
Buffer
A short gap left between bookings for clean-up and small delays.

ul: **Confirm** bookings the day before by phone or message. It cuts down on no-shows.
Repeat the details back to the client when you book.
Never write over another booking; use a pencil if you are on paper and rubbing out.

blocks.note: Only the receptionist and stylist should change a booking, and the change must be shown in the book at once. If two people change the book, clashes follow.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Relaxers, perms, colours and lighteners work by changing the hair. The maker's instructions give the correct time for a safe result.

ul: If a product is left on **too long**, it can burn the scalp, cause hair loss and badly damage the hair.
If it is rinsed **too early**, or the neutralising or rinsing steps are cut short, the result can be patchy and the chemical action may not be properly stopped. That can harm the hair later.
So the time is **never** changed because the salon is busy. Use a **timer**, start it the moment the timed step starts, and write the start and finish times on the client's card.
A stylist who is running late asks for help or moves other clients: she does not shorten the maker's steps.

blocks.h: When things do not go to plan

head: Situation
What to do
rows: The salon is running late
Tell the receptionist at once
She phones or tells the next clients, apologises and offers options
Look for ways to share the work, but never cut safety or processing steps
A client arrives late
Follow the salon's late policy (many allow about 15 minutes)
Check how much time is left before the next client
Offer to do a shorter service, or rebook, and explain politely
A client cancels
Thank her; update the book
Offer the free slot to someone on the waiting list or a walk-in
A client does not show or call
Wait the policy time, then phone her
Mark it as a no-show; use the time for a walk-in or for jobs
Follow the salon's rule about repeat no-shows
A walk-in arrives
Check the book honestly for a gap
Tell her the wait or offer a booking for later; do not squeeze her in and make others wait
A stylist is sick
The supervisor looks at her bookings straight away
Share them with others who have the skills and gaps, without double-booking
The receptionist calls each affected client; offer another stylist, another time or another day
Hold a short huddle; write the new plan where all can see it
A power cut or water lock-off
Check if you can finish safely: no rinse water means no chemical service
Tell clients; rebook if needed
Do jobs that need no power or water, such as restocking and cleaning

blocks.note: Power cuts and water lock-offs happen in Jamaica. Know where the salon's water tank and switches are, keep a torch and spare towels, and agree beforehand with your supervisor what to do. Never start a relaxer or colour if you may not be able to rinse it.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Hold a short **huddle** (a team meeting of a few minutes) at the start of a busy Saturday to share the plan, who is doing what and where the gaps are.
Take your planned breaks. Rest, water and food keep you safe and focused, so you work better afterwards.
If your workload is more than you can finish by closing time, tell your supervisor early and agree what comes first. Do not wait until the last minute.

sections.title: Time wasters, interruptions and asking for help

head: Time waster
How to avoid it
rows: Looking for tools and products
Keep a tidy station; give each tool its own place and return it there; restock at the end of each day.
Personal phone use and long chats
Keep your phone away during services; use it on your break. Politely say 'I will talk to you at my break'.
Poor planning
Check the book in the morning; set up early; keep a to-do list.
Procrastination (putting off tasks you should be doing)
Start with the small job; do cleaning in the gaps rather than letting it pile up.
Interruptions
Ask the receptionist or a colleague to take calls when you are working with a client.
Arriving late or unprepared
Plan the night before; leave early.
Doing things twice
Write things down; confirm what was agreed.

blocks.p: To **delegate** is to give a task to a suitable person. A supervisor delegates to a junior or a colleague. It saves time and builds skills, but you must pick someone with the right skill, explain clearly what is needed and by when, and check the result. Safety-critical tasks, such as a relaxer or a colour service, may not be given to someone who has not been trained.

blocks.h: Saying no politely, and asking for help

ul: If a co-worker asks you to take on a job when you are already full, **thank her for asking, say briefly why you cannot, and offer another time** if you can. Example: 'I am sorry, I have a colour client until three. I can help after that.'
Keep a calm, friendly voice. Do not make excuses or get angry.
If your own workload is too heavy, tell your supervisor **early**. Say what you have to do and how long it will take, and ask her to help you decide what comes first or who can help.
Saying yes to everything leads to rushing, mistakes and skipped safety and hygiene steps.

blocks.note: Asking for help early is a sign of a professional, not a weak one. It protects the client and the business.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A **time log** is a record of what you did and how long each task took. Keep one for a few days or a week.

head: Time
Task
Minutes
Notes
rows: Station set-up
Looked for the towels for 5 minutes
Shampoo and blow-dry
On time
Phone call from a friend
Not work
Looking for the flat iron
Left at another station

ul: Write the **start time** and finish time of each task, including waiting and looking for things.
At the end of the week, add up the time for each kind of task. The result is often different from what you thought.
Find the biggest time wasters and make a plan to cut them down. For example: 40 minutes a day looking for tools means you need a tidy place for each tool.
Compare the time you **planned** for a task with the time it **actually took**.
If a service always takes longer than booked, tell the receptionist to book more time, or practise to get faster, without skipping any steps.
Use what you learn to plan more accurately next time.
Take your breaks. Drink water. Eat properly.
Do not take on more clients than you can serve well. Overbooking causes rushing and stress.
Plan a little time for rest, family and study each week.
At the end of the day, **review**: what went well, what did not, and what is tomorrow's plan?

blocks.note: Time management is not about doing everything faster. It is about doing the right things, in the right order, at the right standard.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: I can explain why managing time matters to clients, the team, the business and me.
I can recognise the signs of poor time management.
I can write a SMART goal and say how it meets each letter.
I can tell short-term, medium-term and long-term goals apart.
I can sort tasks by urgent and important and decide what to do first.
I can plan my day and my week with lists, a calendar, a diary and a timer.
I can read a rota and a simple Gantt chart, and use the 12-hour and 24-hour clock.
I can work out booking times, including processing and clean-up.
I can explain double booking, overbooking, walk-ins and no-shows.
I can explain why chemical service times must never be shortened or stretched.
I can deal with late clients, cancellations, no-shows, walk-ins and staff who are away.
I can name common time wasters and how to avoid them.
I can delegate a suitable task, say no politely and ask for help early.
I can keep a time log and use it to improve.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give a reason for each step. For example: 'I check the appointment book first thing, so that I know which clients need long services and can set up in time.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Using your time well: planning, prioritising and doing the right tasks in the right order.
A goal that is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
A task that must be done first.
The date or time by which a task must be finished.
A plan of what will happen and when.
A set of tasks done in the same order each time.
The time you work out in advance that a task will take.
Doing good work with the least waste of time and effort.
Putting off tasks you should be doing.
Give a task to a suitable person.
A list showing who works when.
A chart that shows tasks as bars along a timeline.
Two clients booked with one stylist at the same time.
Booking more clients than the stylists can serve.
A client who comes without an appointment.
A client who books but does not come or call.
The time a chemical product stays on the hair, as the maker says.
A record of what you did and how long each task took.

c1.title: A long booking in Portmore
c1.text: At a salon in Portmore, receptionist Lorna books Miss Dawkins with stylist Sherika at 9:00 a.m. for a colour, a cut and a blow-dry. The salon's service times are: colour application 40 minutes, processing 35 minutes, shampoo and conditioning 15 minutes, cut 40 minutes, blow-dry 30 minutes, and 10 minutes to clean and reset afterwards. Lorna then books Mr. Reid with Sherika for a 40-minute cut at 9:15 a.m., because Miss Dawkins's colour will be 'processing'.

c2.title: Jodian's time log
c2.text: Trainee Jodian keeps a time log for one day. It shows: 35 minutes looking for tools and products, 25 minutes on her phone, 20 minutes chatting with friends, 15 minutes waiting for the hood dryer, and 5 hours 10 minutes on services. She says she is always rushing and often skips cleaning until the end of the day.

c3.title: Clients who are late or absent
c3.text: On a Monday, a salon's rule is that a client more than 15 minutes late may be asked to rebook or to take a shorter service. Ms. Alicia Gray booked a 3:00 p.m. relaxer touch-up, which takes 90 minutes. At 3:20 p.m. she has not arrived and has not phoned. The next client is due at 4:30 p.m. A walk-in, Mr. Peart, asks for a 30-minute cut. The stylist is free.

c4.title: Marlon's study plan
c4.text: Marlon works on Saturdays at a shop in Mandeville and attends the Centre on weekdays. His practical assessment is in three weeks and he is behind on practising. He writes three goals: A, 'I will do better in the assessment'; B, 'I will practise the assessment cut on a practice head on Tuesday and Thursday evenings, 45 minutes each, so that I can finish it in 40 minutes by the end of the month'; C, 'I will study hard soon'.

c5.title: A weekly rota
c5.text: A salon is open from 8:30 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. Stylist Kemoy works 08:00 to 16:30 and stylist Natasha works 09:30 to 18:00. Each takes a 45-minute lunch break. The owner wants at least one stylist working at all times during opening hours.

questions.q: How long does Miss Dawkins's whole service take, not counting the clean-up?
o: 2 hours 30 minutes
2 hours 10 minutes
2 hours 40 minutes
1 hour 40 minutes
questions.why: Add every step: 40 + 35 + 15 + 40 + 30 = 160 minutes, which is 2 hours 40 minutes. The processing time counts, because the client is in the chair or waiting.

questions.q: What is wrong with Lorna's booking of Mr. Reid at 9:15 a.m.?
o: Sherika is still applying Miss Dawkins's colour then and cannot cut him
Lorna may not book a second client until the first one has finished
A cut cannot be done in a salon while any colour is processing
He should have been booked before Miss Dawkins, since his cut is shorter
questions.why: Miss Dawkins's colour is applied from 9:00 to 9:40, and only then does the 35-minute processing begin. Sherika cannot be applying colour and cutting hair at 9:15, so it is a double booking.

questions.q: What should Lorna do now?
o: Ask Mr. Reid to wait outside until Sherika has finished the colour
Tell Sherika to shorten Miss Dawkins's processing time to fit him in
Leave both bookings and see which client arrives first on the day
Offer Mr. Reid another stylist or time, and update the book
questions.why: A clash must be fixed before the day: move one booking to another stylist or time, tell the client politely and write the change in the book. Processing time is never shortened to catch up.

questions.q: Sherika starts at 9:00 a.m. and has no other client. At what time can the next client sit in her chair, allowing for the clean-up?
questions.why: Service 160 minutes from 9:00 a.m. ends at 11:40 a.m.; adding 10 minutes for clean-up gives 11:50 a.m.

questions.q: How many minutes did Jodian lose to the four time wasters in her log?
o: 110 minutes
95 minutes
60 minutes
75 minutes
questions.why: 35 + 25 + 20 + 15 = 95 minutes, which is 1 hour 35 minutes: a large part of a working day.

questions.q: Which change will save Jodian the most time?
o: Asking her friends not to talk to her at any time
Skipping the clean-up between clients, to catch up
Using her phone only at the end of the day, whatever the situation
A tidy tray with a fixed place for every tool, returned after use
questions.why: The biggest single waste is 35 minutes looking for tools. A fixed place for each one solves that. Skipping clean-up breaks hygiene, and the other two options do not address the biggest cause.

questions.q: Jodian always leaves cleaning until the end of the day. What is the best habit instead?
o: Do small cleaning jobs in the gaps between clients
Do all of the cleaning on Friday afternoon, when the salon is quiet
Ask a new trainee to do all of the cleaning for the whole team
Clean only when a client or the supervisor complains about it
questions.why: Small jobs done in gaps never pile up, and the station is always ready. Leaving them is procrastination, and handing it all to a trainee is not fair.

questions.q: What should the stylist do at 3:20 p.m. about Ms. Gray?
o: Start the relaxer on a model in her place so that no time is lost
Cancel her booking at once without trying to reach her at all
Phone her, then follow the salon's no-show rule if she is not reached
Wait quietly at her chair until she arrives, however late she turns out to be
questions.why: She is already beyond the 15-minute rule. The stylist phones her, then follows the salon's no-show policy and uses the time well. Waiting indefinitely wastes the time of the whole team.

questions.q: What is the best way to use the free time?
o: Let the stylist use the time for her phone while she waits
Send Mr. Peart away, because he has not got a booking today
Keep the stylist free in case Ms. Gray arrives later on
Offer Mr. Peart a cut now, as it fits before 4:30 p.m.
questions.why: A 30-minute walk-in fits in the gap and uses the stylist's time. Keep an eye on the clock, because Ms. Gray's relaxer would need 90 minutes.

questions.q: Ms. Gray arrives at 3:55 p.m. and wants her 90-minute service. What is the best response?
o: Explain politely and offer a shorter service or a new time
Do her relaxer anyway, and let the 4:30 p.m. client wait her turn
Shorten the relaxer processing time so that it finishes by 4:30 p.m.
Ask the 4:30 p.m. client to come back later without telling her why
questions.why: A 90-minute service cannot finish before 4:30 p.m. The salon's late rule exists to protect the other client. Processing times are never shortened.

questions.q: Which of Marlon's goals is SMART?
o: C
A and C
B
A
questions.why: Goal B is specific (the assessment cut), measurable (40 minutes), achievable (two evenings), relevant (the assessment) and time-bound (the end of the month).

questions.q: Studying for the assessment is important but not urgent today. What should Marlon do?
o: Practise only if he has nothing else to do
Plan regular practice times in his week and keep to them
Wait until the day before and do all the practice at once
Drop the practice, because it is not urgent
questions.why: Important but not urgent tasks need planned time, or they become emergencies. Last-minute practice is poor and stressful.

questions.q: Marlon's Saturday work and practice both want the same evening. What is the best action?
o: Move practice to another evening and tell his employer in good time
Skip the practice this week and just hope that the assessment goes well
Cancel work without telling the employer, to keep the evening free
Do both at once, but give each of them only half of the time
questions.why: Planning in a diary shows clashes early. Moving one task and telling others in good time keeps promises and the goal.

questions.q: How long does Kemoy work, taking out her lunch break?
o: 7 hours 15 minutes
8 hours 15 minutes
7 hours 45 minutes
8 hours 30 minutes
questions.why: 08:00 to 16:30 is 8 hours 30 minutes. Taking out 45 minutes leaves 7 hours 45 minutes.

questions.q: What is Natasha's finishing time on the 12-hour clock?
questions.why: After 12:00, subtract 12: 18:00 is 6:00 p.m.

questions.q: The owner wants at least one stylist working at all times. How should the two lunch breaks be set?
o: At the same time, so that the two stylists can eat together
Both late in the day, whenever each of them happens to be free
Skipped on busy days so that both can stay at their stations
Staggered, so only one is away at a time, in the overlap
questions.why: Both stylists are on duty only between 09:30 and 16:30. Staggering breaks in that period keeps one stylist always working.

questions.q: Who is alone in the salon, and when?
o: Kemoy only, from 08:30 to 09:00, when the salon first opens
Neither of them is ever alone while the salon is open to clients
Kemoy until 09:30, and Natasha from 16:30 until closing
Natasha from the opening time until 09:30, and Kemoy after 16:30
questions.why: Kemoy starts at 08:00 and Natasha at 09:30, so Kemoy is alone first; Kemoy leaves at 16:30 and Natasha stays until 18:00.

questions.q: A junior asks you to take her cleaning duty while you are behind with your own work. What is the best reply?
o: Tell her it is not your job and walk away without another word
Thank her, say you cannot right now, and offer help later
Do it quietly, even though you will fall further behind on your own
Say nothing and ignore her request until she stops asking you
questions.why: Say no politely, give a short reason and offer another time. Taking on more than you can manage leads to mistakes.

questions.q: Which task is urgent but not important for a stylist who is working with a client?
o: Rinsing a relaxer when the maker's time is up
Dealing with a client's burning scalp at once
Preparing the station for a client due in ten minutes
Answering a call the receptionist can take
questions.why: The phone is urgent because it is ringing, but it is not important enough to leave a client, and someone else can answer it. The others are urgent and important.

questions.q: What is the best way to estimate how long a new service will take you?
o: Time yourself on a practice head and note the maker's guidance
Always book twice the time, even if it is not needed
Use the time from a video made by a stylist in another country
Guess from how long the same service looked when someone else did it
questions.why: Timing yourself gives a real figure for your own skill. Over time you can update the estimate and compare plan with actual.
